title: Too costly, compared to what?
principle: When they say "too costly", ask "compared to what?"

screens.text: Remember Nirma from Unit 1? In the early 1980s, Nirma powder sold at ₹7 a kilo, and Surf cost ₹28. Surf could not match that price. So in 1984, Surf's TV ads brought in a sharp, careful housewife called Lalitaji. She never said Surf was cheap.

screens.prompt: Surf cost four times as much as Nirma. What do you think Lalitaji told shoppers?

options.label: Surf was on sale this week
Buying cheap is not the same as buying good

screens.why: Her famous line in Hindi, "Surf ki kharidari mein hi samajhdari hai", means smart buying is buying Surf. The idea behind it: buying cheap is not the same as buying good. She made shoppers think about what they got, not the price on the packet.

screens.title: The reference price
screens.text: Every buyer has a price in their head to compare with. It's called the reference price. Shoppers compared ₹28 with ₹7, and Surf lost. Lalitaji made them compare what they got. So when a buyer says "too costly", don't cut your price. Ask: "Compared to what?"

screens.prompt: A customer says your ₹300 haircut is "too costly". What should you say first?

options.label: "Our barbers trained in Mumbai, you know."
"Which price are you comparing it with?"

screens.why: Yes. First find out what they compare with. If it's a ₹60 roadside cut, you can show what's different. If it's the salon next door at ₹250, you know where you stand.

wrong.a: You cut ₹50 before you know what they're comparing with. They might be thinking of ₹280. Ask first: "Which price are you comparing it with?"
wrong.b: That may be true, but you don't know their comparison yet. If they're thinking of a ₹60 roadside cut, Mumbai training won't help. Ask first.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Surf's problem can turn up at your café deal too. It's March. In the two-week trial, he took 10 brownies a day, and they sold out most evenings. Now he wants a monthly deal. But he says ₹45 a brownie is "too costly".

screens.prompt: A slice costs him ₹30 and sells at ₹50. Your ₹45 brownie sells at ₹80. What does he keep per brownie, compared with a slice?
screens.why: Exactly. He keeps ₹20 on a slice (₹50 − ₹30) and ₹35 on a brownie (₹80 − ₹45). That's ₹15 more on each brownie. He was comparing what he pays, not what he keeps.

wrong.a: That's ₹45 − ₹30: you compared what he pays, as he did. Now look at what he keeps: ₹80 − ₹45 is ₹35 on a brownie, ₹50 − ₹30 is ₹20 on a slice. ₹15 more.
wrong.c: Check both sums: ₹80 − ₹45 is ₹35 on a brownie, and ₹50 − ₹30 is ₹20 on a slice. The difference is ₹15.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six replies to "too costly". For each one, tell me: does it change what he compares, or just cut the price?

items.text: Show what he keeps on a brownie and on a slice
Take ₹5 off each brownie this month
Show how fast your brownies sold out in the trial
Agree to ₹40 if he signs today
Show the chain café's real ₹70 brownie price
Give him the first week free

screens.why: Nicely done. The first kind shows a fairer comparison: what he keeps, how fast they sell, a real price elsewhere. The second kind just takes money out of your pocket.

screens.prompt: Imagine you drop to ₹35 a brownie to close the deal. Later, you want ₹45 again. What's the likely problem?

options.label: He now sees ₹35 as your real price
He will want fewer brownies each day
He will ask for more time to pay

screens.why: Right. You saw this in Unit 3: a discount makes a good product look cheap. Once he pays ₹35, going back to ₹45 feels like a price rise.

wrong.b: He may not cut his order. The real problem is the price. Remember Unit 3: a discount makes a good product look cheap. ₹35 becomes your price in his head.
wrong.c: Paying later is a different problem. Remember Unit 3: a discount makes a good product look cheap. ₹35 becomes your price in his head.

screens.setup: It's late March. The owner wants 70 brownies a week, as in the trial, but says ₹45 is too costly. Each brownie costs you ₹20. He sells it at ₹80. His cake slices cost him ₹30 and sell at ₹50.
screens.question: What do you do?

options.label: Drop to ₹35 a brownie to keep the deal
options.outcome: He agrees at once. 70 brownies leave you ₹15 each: ₹1,050 a week. A month later, his friend's café asks you for ₹35 too.
options.why: You beat his comparison on price, but he was comparing the wrong things. Now ₹35 is your price in two cafés.
options.better: Ask what he compares with, then show what he keeps on each brownie.

options.label: Keep ₹45 and tell him your brownies are worth it
options.outcome: He isn't sure, so he orders 50 a week instead of 70. You keep ₹25 on each: ₹1,250 a week.
options.why: Holding your price was right, but "worth it" is only your word. He needed to see the numbers for himself.
options.better: Ask what he compares with, then show what he keeps on each brownie.

options.label: Ask what he compares with, and work it out together
options.outcome: He sees ₹35 on a brownie against ₹20 on a slice. "So the costly one earns me more!" He signs for 70 a week at ₹45. You keep ₹25 on each: ₹1,750 a week.
options.why: You changed what he compared: not what he pays, but what he keeps. Your price stayed the same, and now he sees it as fair.

screens.text: When a buyer says "too costly", ask: compared to ___? Then show a fairer ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Lalitaji moved shoppers from price per kilo to what they got for it. You moved the café from what he pays to what he keeps.

summary: The reference price: every price is judged against another one.
When a buyer says "too costly", ask "compared to what?" before you cut anything.
Show a fairer, true comparison: cost per use, what they keep, or a real price elsewhere.

cards.front: A buyer says your price is too costly. What do you say first?
cards.back: Find their reference price first. Then show a fairer comparison.

cards.front: A shop buys your ₹45 item and sells it at ₹80. A rival's ₹30 item sells at ₹50. Which earns the shop more?
cards.back: Compare what the shop keeps, not what it pays.

cards.front: Surf cost ₹28 a kilo, Nirma ₹7. What did Lalitaji get shoppers to compare instead?
options: What they got for the money
cards.back: She changed the reference: smart buying is about what you get, not the packet price.
